newsitem.title: UK: UK fund industry can grow global business - report.
newsitem.headline: UK fund industry can grow global business - report.

text.p: The fund management industry in Britain, managing an estimated 2.0 trillion stg by end-1996, is well placed to maintain and enlarge its position as a leading global financial centre, a report from British Invisibles shows.

The privately-sponsored body said the UK retained a strong international orientation, a skilled labour force and a liberal operating environment that would help UK firms take advantage of key future developments in fund management "particularly in international markets where growth prospects look strongest".
The industry contributes some 2.7 billion stg or 0.4 percent of GDP to the UK economy and employs some 35,000 people.

Overseas earnings were estimated at 425 million stg in 1995, but that did not reflect overseas earnings from fund management activities or their contribution to an efficient capital market "which mobilises and allocates the nation's savings".

Of the 1.8 trillion stg of identified assets, two-thirds are funds managed on behalf of institutional clients and a quarter on behalf of international clients. The remaining one tenth is private client funds.
The value of institutional client funds has increased fourfold in real terms since 1980, the report said.

"The 500 billion stg managed in the UK on behalf of overseas clients gives the UK a much greater prominance as an international fund management centre than the size of its domestic assets would indicate," British Invisibles said.
Within the UK, 38 percent of funds managed are run by insurance companies and another 38 percent by investment banks. Independent firms manage 16 percent and self-managed pension funds eight percent.
Fund data company InterSec notes that the UK accounts for 48 of the largest 250 fund management companies outside the U.S.

A recent wave of mergers and acquisitions, many with U.S. investment firms, has "heightened the trend towards concentration of assets in a number of large groups," the report quoted InterSec as saying.
London ranks as the second largest city by value of domestic institutional equity portfolios, second only to Tokyo, with American funds spread across a number of centres.

The City, as the financial centre is known, is well placed to manage other countries' non-domestic portfolios "particularly if funded pensions are developed elsewhere", as it already manages two thirds of cross border appointments in Europe from organisations contracting out their fund management business.

The report noted that the establishment of OEICs (Open Ended Investment Companies) from the beginning of this month would also allow UK managers to capture for London the European mutual fund business that until now has gone mostly to Luxembourg.
OEICs offer an investment fund structure familiar to most European players but slightly different from the funds established in the UK.
